## Near-duplicate companion — second worked Task 2 version

`ROmQsqmeUB8` repeats the plan → write → check framework and the same sleep question/student case as `aIqBxtrUodQ`. A normalized transcript comparison found substantial sequence overlap (about 82%); the cuts differ in the amount and wording of the sample-essay feedback. Treat it as a near-duplicate/alternate edit, not an independent strategy. The useful extra details are included here so the second transcript is accounted for.

### Distinct case details to retain

- The prompt’s broad subject is sleep; its specific comparison is sleep now versus in the past. The instructions ask why people sleep less and what effects that has. The learner’s first draft discusses causes when answering the effects part, illustrating why planning must translate each instruction into a separate answer goal. ([2:00–5:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ROmQsqmeUB8&t=120s); [24:00–27:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ROmQsqmeUB8&t=1440s))
- The worked plan selects two straightforward points (people work more; reduced sleep contributes to fatigue), then develops each with explanation and relevant support. The student’s basketball example is presented as something she had read; verify factual examples before teaching them as evidence. Avoid creating a second paragraph point by relabeling the same “busy lifestyle” idea with “secondly.” ([9:00–12:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ROmQsqmeUB8&t=540s); [18:00–27:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ROmQsqmeUB8&t=1080s))
- The introduction critique rejects copying generic openings such as “Nowadays…” and “This essay will discuss…” without knowing what each sentence contributes. Teach a faithful, specific paraphrase and a clear answer preview when useful; the exact formula shown is one worked option. ([13:00–18:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ROmQsqmeUB8&t=780s))
- The student’s draft uses conspicuous words such as *phenomenon*, *myriad*, and *plethora* inaccurately, adds connectors that do not signal a real relationship, and avoids repeating *sleep* by choosing unsuitable alternatives. Teach accuracy and clear relationships first; repetition of a precise key term is better than a meaning-changing synonym. ([17:00–24:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ROmQsqmeUB8&t=1020s); [35:00–40:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ROmQsqmeUB8&t=2100s))
- The instructor reports that roughly 90% of this learner’s errors involved articles and shows article practice plus a final check for recurring and careless errors. Keep the diagnosis individual; the percentage is an unverified case claim, not a rule for other learners. The promised band change and course outcomes are not independently verified. ([30:00–35:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ROmQsqmeUB8&t=1800s))

## Interactive makeover: prompt scope and controlled development

The prompt asks whether governments and individuals spend too much on **national celebrations**, with New Year and religious festivals as examples. In the activity, a wedding-only answer is rejected because it answers a related personal topic rather than the defined national category; the named festivals illustrate the category but need not all be discussed. Build a prompt-analysis exercise around **population + action + scope + instruction** and ask students to explain why plausible ideas do or do not answer it. ([0:00–5:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9t1j4a6CzVk&t=0s))

For this agree/disagree prompt, the instructor selects a clear side and two developable reasons (public events can attract visitors; shared time with family can make personal spending worthwhile). The video compares four-idea plans with a narrower outline. The transferable lesson is to cover every task requirement, then develop a small set of relevant ideas; one-sided or two-sided structure depends on the prompt and should not become a universal rule. “Simple ideas” means easy to explain, not unsupported assertions. ([5:00–10:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9t1j4a6CzVk&t=300s); [17:00–18:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9t1j4a6CzVk&t=1020s))

Teach the introduction as a compact orientation: answer the asked question, state the position, and preview the reasons if that helps the reader. Avoid a dramatic “hook” that delays the answer or memorized padding. Paraphrase the meaning accurately; do not replace each source word with a thesaurus synonym. A body paragraph can then reuse one planned reason as its topic sentence, explain the relationship in plain terms, and add an example that demonstrates that same point. If the writer needs an examiner to ask follow-up questions to understand an explanation, simplify it. ([13:00–25:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9t1j4a6CzVk&t=780s); [28:00–35:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9t1j4a6CzVk&t=1680s))

The worked first body uses government spending and tourism; the second develops family time. The student’s first attempt adds capitalism, productivity, urban life, and wellbeing to the same paragraph, making the line of reasoning hard to follow. Keep one paragraph centered on one principal idea, remove details that create separate claims, and verify examples against the prompt. The student’s St. Patrick’s Day and Dubai-fireworks examples illustrate the exercise; the video does not independently verify their factual details. ([32:00–43:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9t1j4a6CzVk&t=1920s))

Conclude by restating the established position and reasons without adding an idea. Review grammar, spelling, and punctuation, then check vocabulary for unnecessary repetition or inaccurate word choice. Practise editing independently on an unaided response; keep the source’s suggested 5–10-minute planning window as an individual coaching estimate, not an official time quota. The band-6.5-to-8/9 transformation and the learner’s wish to move abroad are a video case and promotional framing, not independently verified score or migration outcomes. ([43:00–48:22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9t1j4a6CzVk&t=2580s))

- [40:00–46:01 — State the opinion again and conclude by summarizing the established argument](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kpRmyUNDmwc&t=2400s)

## Two long makeovers: audit the task before editing sentences

### Mobile-phone essay: answer both parts precisely

The worked task asks why children spend substantial time on mobile phones and whether the advantages outweigh the disadvantages. The draft begins with a generic “Nowadays … hot topic” sentence, uses *adolescents* where the prompt says *children*, gives reasons without a clear answer to the positive/negative judgment, and ends with a conclusion that still does not make that judgment explicit. Teach learners to mark each required answer, keep the prompt’s population and scope, state a position, and carry that position consistently through the introduction, body, and conclusion. A background sentence is optional only if it contributes useful, accurate context; it is not an obligatory formula. ([0:00–9:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hS7J1fNOulg&t=0s); [16:00–23:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hS7J1fNOulg&t=960s))

In the revised answer, one paragraph explains why children use phones, and the next develops the negative judgment with a reason and example. The reusable procedure is **answer the task → choose one relevant reason → explain why it supports the position → illustrate it → check the link to the task**. A concrete personal, hypothetical, or factual example can work if it supports the point; IELTS does not require statistics or ban personal examples. Do not use an uncertain percentage as fact. The draft’s “89%” phone-game statistic is rejected in the video; several claims used in the instructor’s replacement example are also not verified here, so substitute checked evidence or a clearly hypothetical illustration. ([9:00–15:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hS7J1fNOulg&t=540s); [32:00–44:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hS7J1fNOulg&t=1920s); [official Task 2 format](https://ielts.org/take-a-test/test-types/ielts-academic-test/ielts-academic-format-writing))

The vocabulary comparison is useful for teaching precision: a wider range is valuable when it conveys the intended meaning accurately, but *progeny*, *offspring*, or *pedagogical* may distort scope or register when the writer simply means *children* or *useful*. Repeat a precise key word when a true alternative is unavailable. For grammar, the instructor highlights recurring article and countability errors. Turn those into learner-specific error patterns and a short repair exercise rather than asserting that every learner has only one or two weak areas. ([23:00–32:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hS7J1fNOulg&t=1380s))

The tutor’s band labels and exact essay-score predictions are not independently verified. The official descriptors do say that the **majority of sentences are error-free** at Band 8 for Grammatical Range and Accuracy, while Band 7 describes error-free sentences as frequent. Do not turn that descriptor into a mechanical 50% error-count formula for scoring a full essay: IELTS assesses four criteria, and trained examiners judge the response against the complete descriptors. ([official Writing band descriptors](https://ielts.org/cdn/ielts-guides/ielts-writing-band-descriptors.pdf); [IELTS scoring and criterion weighting](https://www.ielts.org/take-a-test/your-results/ielts-scoring-in-detail))

### Professionals’ mobility: cover two views and give the requested opinion

The prompt asks candidates to discuss both views about trained professionals working in their home country or abroad **and give their opinion**. The instructor breaks that into three questions: why someone might be expected to stay; why someone might want freedom to move; and which view the writer supports. An introduction can briefly explain both positions and state the writer’s own view, then one body paragraph can develop each view. In the conclusion, summarize the positions and restate the chosen opinion without adding a new reason. First person is appropriate when the task asks for the writer’s opinion; a blanket ban on *I think* or *I believe* is not an official rule. ([2:00–9:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kpRmyUNDmwc&t=120s); [25:00–31:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kpRmyUNDmwc&t=1500s); [40:00–46:01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kpRmyUNDmwc&t=2400s))

The before/after case demonstrates the difference between naming a point and developing it. For example, a claim about public investment in training needs an explanation of why that supports a duty to remain, then a fitting example. The opposing paragraph should explain why professional mobility benefits the individual and support that claim. Use a reader check such as “So what?” to see whether more explanation is needed. Each paragraph should stay centered on its reason, and its example should support that reason. ([31:00–40:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kpRmyUNDmwc&t=1860s))

If a personal example is too narrow, the writer can generalize the relevant point carefully; however, personal examples are not categorically unsuitable. The tutor’s claims about UK physician training, oil-rich countries, salaries, employment, and the relative success of migration examples are not independently checked. Do not teach them as facts; verify evidence or use an illustrative hypothetical. Use simple, accurate language and avoid memorized openings, vague “hot topic” statements, lists of loosely related ideas, and a conclusion that introduces a surprise opinion. The advertised Band 6-to-8 transformation and career/migration outcomes are promotional or anecdotal, not official score evidence.

### Score claims and descriptor use across both videos

Both teachers interpret the criteria to identify real issues such as task coverage, a consistent position, paragraph development, lexical accuracy, and recurring grammar. Keep the criteria but do not adopt the videos’ exact candidate bands, 50%-error scoring cutoffs, claims that most writers have only one or two grammar weaknesses, or the claim that one formula reliably changes a score. IELTS states that Task 2 uses Task Response, Coherence and Cohesion, Lexical Resource, and Grammatical Range and Accuracy; each criterion is weighted equally within the task. Task 2 itself weighs more than Task 1 in the Writing score. ([IELTS official scoring](https://www.ielts.org/take-a-test/your-results/ielts-scoring-in-detail); [official Writing criteria](https://ielts.org/cdn/ielts-guides/ielts-writing-key-assessment-criteria.pdf))

- [0:00–4:30 — Interpret the discuss-both-views-and-opinion prompt; choose specific, supportable ideas](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1alDRNuVLs&t=0s)
- [4:30–9:40 — Match the essay plan to every instruction; compare structures and build a brief outline](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1alDRNuVLs&t=270s)
- [9:40–15:45 — Select and explain points for each view; plan examples and time](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1alDRNuVLs&t=580s)
- [15:45–23:55 — Paraphrase accurately and introduce both sides plus the writer’s view](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1alDRNuVLs&t=945s)
- [23:55–35:55 — Develop both body paragraphs with explanation, examples, and a consistent position](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1alDRNuVLs&t=1435s)
- [35:55–38:18 — Conclude consistently and review vocabulary, punctuation, and grammar](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1alDRNuVLs&t=2155s)

## Cosmetic-surgery discussion essay: preserve meaning while developing both views

**Transcript:** [From 6.5 to 8.0: IELTS Writing Makeover](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1alDRNuVLs), full English transcript in Glasp Reader through 38:18; YouTube captions were unavailable.

The worked prompt asks whether there should be an age limit for cosmetic surgery or whether young adults should be free to choose, and requires discussion of both views plus the writer’s opinion. Begin by translating each instruction into a coverage check. Select ideas that are directly relevant, specific enough to explain, plausible, and easy to support; avoid claims that are too vague (“they are not mature”) or absolute (“it always harms them”). In this example, social-media influence and later regret support the age-limit side, while confidence and mental wellbeing support personal choice. Learners need not agree personally with every side they explain, but they must represent the question accurately.

The lesson compares structures by whether they help the reader see both perspectives and the writer’s view. Its four-paragraph model (introduction, one body paragraph for each view, conclusion) is a usable scaffold for this prompt, not a universal requirement. A brief plan should record the central point, its explanation, and a relevant example for each paragraph; the instructor recommends ten planning minutes and five minutes of checking, but these are coaching targets to adapt to the learner and the test clock. Check that the logic would be clear to an unfamiliar reader. The body demonstration moves from claim to explanation, example, and the writer’s response; the example needs to support the specific point, not merely share the same topic.

Paraphrase for meaning rather than word replacement. The lesson catches several scope shifts: *cosmetic surgery* is not always interchangeable with *plastic surgery* or the broader *cosmetic enhancements*; *young adults* should not be widened to *young people*; and “gaining precedence” means gaining priority or importance, not becoming more popular. If no accurate alternative comes readily, repeat the key term. In the introduction, paraphrase the topic, briefly introduce both views, and state the opinion. Keep the position consistent across the two body paragraphs and conclusion; conclude by recapping the views and restating the same position.

Use any remaining review time to check whether every task demand is covered, the paraphrase preserves the prompt, examples fit their claims, and grammar, spelling, capitalization, and punctuation are clear. Vocabulary variation is optional and should happen only when the replacement is accurate; repeated key words are safer than a thesaurus substitution that changes meaning. The title’s 6.5-to-8 outcome, the predicted higher bands, course success claims, the fixed planning minutes, and the instructor’s cultural generalizations are not independently verified and are not exam rules. ([official Writing criteria](https://ielts.org/take-a-test/preparation-resources/writing-test-resources); [official Writing descriptors](https://ielts.org/cdn/ielts-guides/ielts-writing-band-descriptors.pdf))

## Distilled workflow

1. **Classify the task.** The teacher lists opinion, discussion, advantages/disadvantages, problem/solution, causes/solutions, and double/direct questions. Treat these as planning labels, then check every instruction in the actual prompt; prompts can combine requirements.
2. **Narrow the topic to the task.** Identify the broad subject, the specific issue, and what the instruction asks the candidate to do. In the video’s example, the broad subject is government spending, the focused comparison is railways versus roads, and the instruction asks for a degree of agreement. Do not write a general essay about infrastructure.
3. **Generate a few relevant ideas.** Ask a direct question that expresses the prompt, then choose one or two points that answer it and that you can explain. A simple, well-developed idea is more useful than a complicated point that drifts off task. Open-ended brainstorming is one possible tool; the course should teach learners to keep it focused and stop once they have enough material.
4. **Outline before drafting.** Use a dependable structure suited to the prompt. For the video’s opinion example, the outline links the position and two reasons to the introduction, body paragraphs, and conclusion. This creates a route through the essay so the learner can focus on sentence-level writing while drafting.
5. **Write a task-specific introduction.** For an opinion essay, the student example paraphrases the claim, states agreement, and previews two reasons. Avoid padding such as a generic background sentence or a description of what the essay will do. Do not force this exact formula onto every question type.
6. **Develop each body paragraph.** State a central point, explain how it answers the question, then support it with a relevant example. The point and explanation can take more or fewer sentences; see the companion method below for a detailed procedure. The three elements are a planning scaffold, not a sentence quota.
7. **Conclude the argument.** Restate the answer or position when the prompt asks for one, then recap the main reasons. A short signpost such as “In conclusion” is optional. Keep the position and reasons consistent with the essay; do not introduce a new claim, become vague, or force a synonym where the original wording is more precise. Whether a personal position is needed depends on the prompt. ([18:50–20:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NECR879vg-Y&t=1130s); [0:30–6:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Rk8fjwbRGvQ&t=30s))
8. **Check in focused passes.** Build accuracy before test day by identifying recurring grammar problems and practising them directly. During the final review, check language, task coverage, paragraphing, cohesion, word count, and whether the answer remains clear. The companion suggests checking at sentence, paragraph, and whole-essay levels. This is a useful review pattern, not a requirement to inspect every sentence three times; adapt the passes to the learner’s needs and time. Its five-minute final-check window is a practice target, not an official timing rule. ([20:52–26:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NECR879vg-Y&t=1252s); [7:02–10:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Rk8fjwbRGvQ&t=422s))

The 2026 companion makes the planning step more explicit: identify the broad subject, narrow it to the prompt’s specific focus, and translate every instruction into a question that the essay must answer. For a two-part prompt, it contrasts causes with effects; answering the adjacent but unasked question is still a task-response failure. Practise this by labeling the scope and task on several prompts before drafting. ([2:25–5:18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aIqBxtrUodQ&t=145s))

For idea generation, replace open-ended searching with direct prompt questions, then select a small number of relevant points that can be explained and supported. An obvious, familiar idea is sufficient when it answers the task and can be developed; novelty and specialist knowledge are not goals. Do the main thinking before drafting so the writer is not trying to invent ideas while composing sentences. The video cautions against mixing several competing structures; teach learners to choose a suitable structure and practise it, while retaining flexibility across different prompt demands. ([5:18–11:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aIqBxtrUodQ&t=318s))

Its before-and-after essay adds a diagnostic example: the weaker response uses memorized openings and rare-word substitutions, lists several points without development, confuses causes with effects, and introduces new claims in the conclusion. The revision states the answer directly, develops a main point through explanation and relevant support, and summarizes the same answer at the end. Use this as a worked example of diagnosing prompt coverage, paragraph focus, and language control; do not treat the student's reported 6.5 → 8 result as verified or promise the same outcome. ([12:37–29:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aIqBxtrUodQ&t=757s))

During editing, check task response and organization alongside language. Identify a learner’s highest-impact recurring grammar pattern (the source’s example is article use), practise it directly, and proofread using short passes appropriate to the time available. Preserve accurate vocabulary instead of forcing a thesaurus substitute: paraphrase when a genuine equivalent fits, and repeat the key term when alternatives would distort meaning. These are priorities for instruction, not fixed score formulas. ([29:00–39:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aIqBxtrUodQ&t=1740s))

The 13-minute essay walkthrough reinforces the same sequence with a memorable “birthday cake” analogy: the paragraph’s central point is the cake, its explanation is the icing, and relevant examples are the decorations. The useful concept is the logical link from claim to explanation to support; the image is a memory aid, not a mandatory paragraph formula. Its prompt-type → exact scope → answer plan routine overlaps the other guides, and its introduction/body/body/conclusion structure is one novice-friendly option. ([1:00–3:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q_5jmvbwf-g&t=60s); [7:00–10:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q_5jmvbwf-g&t=420s))

The 45-minute interactive lesson applies the method to a two-part causes-and-solutions task. It asks learners to distinguish the topic’s background and time frame from the actual instructions, then check whether each idea is relevant, reasonable, and possible to explain. It rejects an unrelated opinion and separates a cause from an explanation of why something is a problem. In the worked example, the introduction briefly paraphrases the task and previews the causes and solutions; the writer can look back at this outline to stay on track. For this prompt, the instructor groups causes in one body paragraph and solutions in another. That is a workable option, not a requirement to write exactly two causes, exactly two solutions, or four paragraphs. ([0:00–3:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x-_vHUzm3b4&t=0s); [8:00–17:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x-_vHUzm3b4&t=480s); [22:00–26:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x-_vHUzm3b4&t=1320s))

## Companion: interactive traffic-congestion problems-and-solutions essay

The 39-minute [From Band 6.5 to 7.0 in IELTS Writing](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xZ5JkW13Dtk) lesson repeats the interactive planning method with a traffic-congestion prompt:

- [0:00 — Read the task and distinguish problems from causes](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xZ5JkW13Dtk&t=0s)
- [2:00 — Test possible ideas for relevance and development](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xZ5JkW13Dtk&t=120s)
- [8:00 — Build a short plan and paragraph map](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xZ5JkW13Dtk&t=480s)
- [11:00 — Paraphrase accurately and avoid unnatural synonyms](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xZ5JkW13Dtk&t=660s)
- [19:00 — Use the introduction as a mini-plan](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xZ5JkW13Dtk&t=1140s)
- [24:00 — Develop a body paragraph around one focused point](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xZ5JkW13Dtk&t=1440s)
- [30:00 — Conclude, review, and identify grammar patterns](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xZ5JkW13Dtk&t=1800s)

The learner first separates traffic’s problems (lost commuting time and air pollution) from causes of traffic, then compares options by asking whether each directly answers the task and can be explained with a clear reason or example. For this prompt, the demonstration selects two problems and two solutions (public transport and remote work). Treat the number and paragraph arrangement as this answer’s plan, not a universal formula. The prompt’s instructions determine coverage.

The worked introduction uses a plain paraphrase and briefly lists the selected ideas, making it a mini-plan for the body. The essay then develops focused topic sentences with explanation and support, and the conclusion restates the same response. Use that point → explanation → support pattern when it fits; a personal or public example should explain the chosen point rather than merely share the broad topic. An example is useful, not mandatory in every paragraph.

The lesson warns against memorized introductions and unrelated opinion templates, yet also calls its four-paragraph structure something learners should memorize. Teach the problem/solution sequence as a scaffold that makes the task visible; keep it flexible when a prompt’s instructions call for another organization. Its 260–300-word target is a classroom example, not a word-count range to enforce. ([0:00–2:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xZ5JkW13Dtk&t=0s); [8:00–11:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xZ5JkW13Dtk&t=480s); [16:00–20:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xZ5JkW13Dtk&t=960s); [24:00–32:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xZ5JkW13Dtk&t=1440s))

Its final review focuses on the learner’s recurring articles, subject–verb agreement, and punctuation, then recommends learning the relevant rule, practising it, and checking new writing. This is an individual diagnosis; do not infer error patterns from the candidate’s language background. The teacher also says examiners count error-free sentences and supplies simplified criterion percentages. IELTS descriptors describe grammatical range and accuracy qualitatively; do not teach a fixed error-free-sentence threshold. ([32:00–39:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xZ5JkW13Dtk&t=1920s); [Writing Task 2 band descriptors](https://ielts.org/cdn/ielts-guides/ielts-writing-band-descriptors.pdf); [IELTS Writing resources](https://ielts.org/take-a-test/preparation-resources/writing-test-resources))

## Companion: mobile-phone two-part essay makeover

The 33-minute [From Band 6.5 to 8: IELTS Writing Makeover](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WmAQIHcS87g) works through a two-part positive/negative-development prompt about parents allowing toddlers to use mobile phones:

- [0:00 — Identify the task and test possible ideas](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WmAQIHcS87g&t=0s)
- [4:00 — Choose a structure that answers both parts](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WmAQIHcS87g&t=240s)
- [8:00 — Build a direct introduction and paraphrase accurately](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WmAQIHcS87g&t=480s)
- [18:00 — Develop each main point with explanation and support](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WmAQIHcS87g&t=1080s)
- [29:00 — Revisit the introduction in the conclusion](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WmAQIHcS87g&t=1740s)
- [30:00 — Check word count, grammar, and vocabulary](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WmAQIHcS87g&t=1800s)

Translate each instruction into an answer goal. The demonstration selects one reason parents give phones (to keep toddlers occupied) and one position on the effect (educational apps can make it positive), then answers both in the introduction. Its weaker samples either answer the wrong question or introduce a factual claim about permanent eye damage that would be hard to support. Teach a relevant, explainable position; learners do not need the examiner to agree with them, but examples should support the claim and not invent evidence.

In the paraphrase exercise, “toddlers” is narrower than “kids,” and “for an extended period every day” is more specific than simply “use phones.” Keep the original scope and frequency. If there is no safe, natural equivalent, repeat the key word rather than use an inaccurate synonym. The introduction should preview the actual answers; a hook, opposing-view discussion, or memorized phrase is unnecessary unless the prompt calls for it. ([8:00–18:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WmAQIHcS87g&t=480s))

The two body paragraphs use topic sentence → explanation → example: parents may use a phone while occupied with cooking or other tasks, and educational apps may teach colors or objects. The conclusion restates the same answer. This is one useful way to develop the prompt, not a required two-body formula. The transcript’s 260–300-word target is an example; the official minimum is 250 words. Its advice to practice paraphrasing on 10–20 prompts weekly is a personal routine, not a universal quota. ([18:00–30:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WmAQIHcS87g&t=1080s); [IELTS Academic Writing format](https://ielts.org/take-a-test/test-types/ielts-academic-test/ielts-academic-format-writing))

Final review can check whether punctuation and grammar errors recur, then turn one pattern into a short rule-and-practice exercise. The candidate’s comma-splice issue is specific to that draft; do not infer it or any other weakness from her band in Speaking, nationality, or language background. The teacher’s fixed error-free sentence count is not an official scoring threshold, and errors in one criterion do not automatically determine the others. ([27:00–33:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WmAQIHcS87g&t=1620s); [Writing Task 2 band descriptors](https://ielts.org/cdn/ielts-guides/ielts-writing-band-descriptors.pdf))

## Companion: five-step essay lesson with worked planning and review

The 40-minute [From Band 6.5 to 9 in ONE Writing Lesson](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UzjW8ycJu9U) teaches an agree/disagree essay about whether music connects people from different backgrounds:

- [0:00 — Read the question and distinguish its general topic from its specific task](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UzjW8ycJu9U&t=0s)
- [3:00 — Generate a few relevant idea options](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UzjW8ycJu9U&t=180s)
- [6:00 — Select ideas that answer the prompt and can be developed](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UzjW8ycJu9U&t=360s)
- [10:00 — Build a four-part plan from the selected ideas](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UzjW8ycJu9U&t=600s)
- [12:00 — Plan the introduction, body paragraphs, and conclusion](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UzjW8ycJu9U&t=720s)
- [22:00 — Draft the introduction and body paragraphs](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UzjW8ycJu9U&t=1320s)
- [29:00 — Complete the conclusion and check word count](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UzjW8ycJu9U&t=1740s)
- [35:00 — Review vocabulary, grammar, and punctuation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UzjW8ycJu9U&t=2100s)

The transferable sequence is **understand the task → generate a small set of ideas → select relevant, explainable points → make a brief structure plan → draft → review**. The lesson first distinguishes the broad subject from the exact question, then gives idea prompts: the learner’s immediate view, a simple familiar point, a personal or observed situation, and a “what might people commonly say?” prompt. These are options for generating possibilities, not a required brainstorm ritual. Select ideas by whether they answer the prompt and have a clear explanation or example; novelty and examiner agreement are not goals.

Once ideas are chosen, plan one main point for each body paragraph. The demonstrated opinion essay uses an introduction (accurate paraphrase, position, brief preview), two body paragraphs (topic sentence, explanation, relevant example or support), and a conclusion (same position and reasons restated). Treat this as a useful response scaffold, not a universal essay count. A quick final check against the original task can catch a missed instruction; avoid the source’s absolute “one-way door” metaphor if a learner discovers that the plan does not answer the prompt.

During drafting, explain the idea for a reader who cannot ask follow-up questions. A child or unfamiliar-reader check can expose missing links, but it should prompt clarification rather than oversimplification. The demonstration first comes in at 202 words; it adds a relevant detail and explicit link to the answer, reaching 261. This is a useful lesson in developing underdeveloped support, not a license to pad or repeat ideas merely to meet length. IELTS Academic Task 2 requires at least 250 words. ([Writing Task 2 band descriptors](https://ielts.org/cdn/ielts-guides/ielts-writing-band-descriptors.pdf); [IELTS Academic Writing format](https://ielts.org/take-a-test/test-types/ielts-academic-test/ielts-academic-format-writing))

The final review has two passes: first check whether repeated vocabulary can be varied accurately, then check grammar and punctuation patterns. Keep accurate repetition when a safe alternative is unavailable; do not spend the entire review searching for sophisticated synonyms. The 5–10-minute planning target, five-minute review window, 12–15-sentence estimate, Family-Feud-style “100 people” prompt, and claim that planning time predicts a higher score are instructor heuristics without a demonstrated basis. The learner’s reported progress and the title’s Band 9 promise are not independently verified. ([18:00–20:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UzjW8ycJu9U&t=1080s); [30:00–40:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UzjW8ycJu9U&t=1800s); [Writing Task 2 band descriptors](https://ielts.org/cdn/ielts-guides/ielts-writing-band-descriptors.pdf))

## Companion: compare the essay decisions, not the band label

The 24-minute [Simple Fixes That Turn a Band 6 Essay Into Band 8](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1aQZ7_tfgps) contrasts a weak and a strong response to an opinion prompt. The practical differences are prompt comprehension before idea generation; a brief plan; simple, relevant ideas; an introduction that accurately paraphrases the task and makes the position and reasons clear; body paragraphs that develop one central reason through explanation and relevant support; consistent links between the introduction and body; a conclusion that restates the same answer; and time to proofread. Its “Google Maps” analogy for planning is a memory aid. The 5–10-minute plan, 25-minute writing, five-minute check, and two-body-paragraph structure are suggested for the demonstration, not fixed IELTS rules. ([1:00–7:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1aQZ7_tfgps&t=60s); [7:00–13:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1aQZ7_tfgps&t=420s); [13:00–22:45](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1aQZ7_tfgps&t=780s))

The comparison reinforces avoiding generic background openings, memorized introductions, a pile of unrelated points, forced high-level words, and new arguments in the conclusion. Judge language by whether it is accurate, appropriate, and helps the reader understand the answer; do not teach the transcript’s unsupported claim that 95% of high-band essay words are simple. The source’s frequency claim that 90% of successful students planned for 5–10 minutes, its comparative success claims, and its advertised band outcomes are not substantiated. ([7:00–13:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1aQZ7_tfgps&t=420s); [17:00–22:45](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1aQZ7_tfgps&t=1020s))

## Companion summaries: one-sentence Task 2 reminder

The 8-minute [IELTS Writing Is HARD Until You Learn This One Sentence](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NZkkd7V2Gek) and its shorter 6-minute companion, [Understand IELTS Writing Task 2 in 5 Minutes](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yvt8RzGNhBc), use the same mnemonic: a good essay clearly answers the question in a logical way, using accurate and appropriate language. Both unpack it into prompt understanding, relevant idea selection, a structure that makes the answer easy to follow, and controlled language. Their examples restate the existing workflow above, so they are recorded as overlap sources rather than a new essay formula. ([0:00–6:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NZkkd7V2Gek&t=0s); [0:00–5:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yvt8RzGNhBc&t=0s))

In the longer lesson, the instructor says the introduction should paraphrase and briefly answer the question, body paragraphs should give a point, explanation, and example, and the conclusion should recap the answer. These are useful functions; the usual two-body structure and the promise that one sentence or template reliably produces Band 7–9 are not official requirements or guarantees. The two lessons’ student essay counts, analysis claims, and score promises are not independently verifiable. ([2:30–6:15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NZkkd7V2Gek&t=150s); [2:00–5:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yvt8RzGNhBc&t=120s))

Its paraphrase exercise makes the meaning check concrete: *literature* can be broader than *books*, and *reluctant* adds a sense of unwillingness that is absent from a neutral statement about reading fewer books. Teach learners to preserve the source meaning and scope, use an accurate collocation where it helps (the lesson's *book readership* example), and retain the key word when a safe equivalent is unavailable. Paraphrasing does not require replacing every word or meeting a word-change percentage. ([17:00–22:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x-_vHUzm3b4&t=1020s))

The worked body sections also reinforce clear topic points, explanation for a reader who cannot ask questions, and relevant concrete support. They demonstrate checking repeated words only after meaning and accuracy are secure. The instructor identifies the learner's punctuation, article, and subject–verb agreement patterns as review targets; treat those as this learner's diagnosis, not a universal error ranking. ([26:00–38:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x-_vHUzm3b4&t=1560s))

## Body-paragraph method from the 36-minute lesson

Keep returning to the exact prompt as you draft. The lesson’s three-part scaffold is **topic sentence → explanation → example**:

1. **Topic sentence:** give the paragraph’s central point in a direct, specific sentence that answers one part of the prompt and connects to the essay plan. Avoid a general background statement that could introduce almost any essay, or a list of several unrelated points. ([1:05–3:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rXVR-nE2jvw&t=65s); [6:04–10:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rXVR-nE2jvw&t=364s))
2. **Explanation:** ask “So what?” and explain why the point matters, how it works, or how it supports the answer. Write for a reader who cannot ask follow-up questions. An analogy such as explaining the idea to a child or someone unfamiliar with the topic can reveal a missing link; use it to check clarity, not to oversimplify the subject. ([15:06–21:25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rXVR-nE2jvw&t=906s))
3. **Example or support:** add a relevant example, evidence, or concrete detail that makes the same point easier to understand. The lesson gives public examples, everyday experience, and personal experience as possible sources. A personal case can illustrate a point, but a single case does not establish a general trend by itself. Make the link to the topic sentence explicit. ([22:18–30:33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rXVR-nE2jvw&t=1338s))

Use this quick review after drafting:

- Does the topic sentence answer a specific part of the prompt?
- Does the explanation show how or why the point supports the answer?
- Does the example illustrate that same point, rather than merely sharing the broad topic?
- Does the paragraph remain consistent with the introduction and the rest of the essay?
- Have I replaced a “shopping list” of ideas with enough development of the selected point?

The source says examples need not be true if plausible. Keep the useful emphasis on relevance and plausibility, but teach learners not to present invented statistics, named studies, or company claims as facts. IELTS guidance says Task 2 examples may draw on the candidate’s own knowledge or experience and assesses how well ideas are developed and supported; an illustrative hypothetical can be made clear as a hypothetical. ([IELTS Academic Writing format](https://ielts.org/take-a-test/test-types/ielts-academic-test/ielts-academic-format-writing); [Writing Task 2 band descriptors](https://ielts.org/cdn/ielts-guides/ielts-writing-band-descriptors.pdf))

## Clarity edits from a learner case

[From Band 6 to 8 Using One Simple Strategy](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=baIkTadn2oA) demonstrates three optional editing prompts: would a reader understand this sentence on the first read; would active voice make the actor and action clearer; and is one sentence trying to carry several different ideas? The worked example turns a dense health-care sentence into two direct sentences. Use these prompts to repair genuine obscurity, not as rules to make every sentence simple or active. Passive voice can be useful, and well-controlled clauses can express relationships and demonstrate grammatical range. The source’s “13-year-old” test, one-idea-per-sentence rule, and Band 6-to-8 outcome are not IELTS requirements or verified score evidence. ([3:00–6:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=baIkTadn2oA&t=180s); [Writing Task 2 band descriptors](https://ielts.org/cdn/ielts-guides/ielts-writing-band-descriptors.pdf))


## Companion: comprehensive Task 2 method lesson

This 28-minute lesson presents the writing process as **plan → draft → check** and names six broad prompt families: opinion, discussion, advantages/disadvantages, problems/solutions, causes/solutions, and direct or double questions. Treat the grouping as a teaching aid; identify the actual instruction and answer every part of the prompt before selecting a structure. The railway-versus-roads example distinguishes the broad subject (government spending), the specific comparison (railways versus roads), and the task instruction (state the degree of agreement). This is a useful prompt-analysis demonstration. ([0:00–4:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9-E8VUGMiqA&t=0s))

The lesson’s “ask a direct question” idea prompt is another way to produce one or two relevant, supportable points quickly. For the example, ask why a government might prioritize railways; select a point the learner can explain rather than generate a long list. Keep the useful warning against unfiltered brainstorming, but do not teach that all brainstorming is useless or that the simplest idea is always best. Screen candidate ideas for direct relevance, development, and clarity. ([4:30–7:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9-E8VUGMiqA&t=270s))

Next, use a structure that fits the question type to turn the selected points into a roadmap. For the demonstrated opinion essay, the introduction paraphrases accurately, states the position, and previews the reasons; the body develops those reasons; the conclusion restates the position and summarizes the reasoning. These are flexible functions, not a required sentence count or a fixed formula for every prompt. Avoid filler openings, memorized paragraphs, and new arguments in the conclusion. The body-paragraph scaffold—point → explanation → example or support—helps develop a point, but learners may adapt it to the task and their reasoning. ([7:30–20:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9-E8VUGMiqA&t=450s))

The final review separates grammar, vocabulary, and task/organization checks. Specific grammar patterns from the learner’s own work can guide repair; vocabulary should be checked for meaning, collocation, and appropriacy; then confirm paragraphing, word count, prompt coverage, position, and cohesion. The repeated sentence/paragraph/whole-essay grammar checks are the instructor’s routine, not a mandatory or validated number of passes. Prioritize the learner’s recurring errors and reserve enough time for the full 60-minute Writing test. The source’s claims that checking will identify a band-limiting error, that most grammar errors cluster in one or two areas, or that a particular structure is trusted because of student success stories are not independently demonstrated. ([20:30–26:45](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9-E8VUGMiqA&t=1230s))

The video describes the four Writing criteria as 25% each. This is correct within a task, but its shorthand needs context: Task 2 is weighted twice as heavily as Task 1 in the overall Writing score. A grammar error does not automatically lower Coherence and Cohesion; score each criterion on its own evidence. The title’s “only method,” guaranteed high-score framing, the instructor’s own writing-speed claims, and paid/free-course promotion are not proof that one method guarantees a result. ([official IELTS Writing scoring](https://ielts.org/take-a-test/your-results/ielts-scoring-in-detail); [official Writing criteria](https://ielts.org/take-a-test/preparation-resources/writing-test-resources); [official Writing format](https://ielts.org/take-a-test/test-types/ielts-academic-test/ielts-academic-format-writing))


## Companion: “The ONLY IELTS Writing Task 2 Strategy You Need” essay comparison

This upload compares two responses to a sugary-drinks prompt. Its useful planning sequence is to identify the question type, distinguish the general topic from the specific issue and instruction, choose relevant ideas, and map them into a prompt-appropriate structure before drafting. The essay comparison illustrates a response that stays focused on the question rather than collecting general topic facts. The source’s alternative to brainstorming—asking one direct question about the prompt and selecting a relevant answer—is a useful option, not proof that all brainstorming fails. Screen ideas for relevance, development, and clarity. ([0:00–7:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4hI-ST678rI&t=0s))

In the opinion-essay example, the weaker draft opens with general background, leaves the position unclear, and tries to use memorized complex vocabulary. The stronger sample paraphrases accurately, states a position, and previews its supporting ideas. In the body, one main point per paragraph is linked to the introduction, explained, and supported with an example. The conclusion restates the position and summarizes the developed reasons rather than adding new material. Teach these as flexible functions matched to the task; do not require one exact number of ideas or a fixed sentence length. ([7:00–21:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4hI-ST678rI&t=420s))

The instructor’s “Band 5–6.5” and “Band 7–9” labels are not independent ratings, and the two worked essays do not establish that all learners in those score groups write the same way. Claims that most higher-scoring students spend 5–10 minutes planning, that 95% of Band 9 vocabulary is simple, or that the comparison guarantees a result are not substantiated in the clip. Keep the core advice—answer the exact prompt, make the position visible, develop linked ideas, and check the response—while grounding assessment in the official criteria. The source’s “one shot, one kill” analogy is dropped from student-facing course content. ([5:00–7:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4hI-ST678rI&t=300s); [official IELTS Writing criteria](https://ielts.org/take-a-test/preparation-resources/writing-test-resources))

## Keep the source’s claims in proportion

- IELTS Task 2 requires at least 250 words, is completed within a 60-minute Writing test, and contributes twice as much as Task 1. These are official format facts. ([IELTS Academic Writing format](https://ielts.org/take-a-test/test-types/ielts-academic-test/ielts-academic-format-writing); [General Training Writing format](https://ielts.org/take-a-test/test-types/ielts-general-training-test/ielts-general-training-format-writing))
- Writing is assessed using Task Response, Coherence and Cohesion, Lexical Resource, and Grammatical Range and Accuracy. Accurate and appropriate vocabulary matters, as does range; the official descriptors do not say that simpler essays inherently score higher. The teacher’s reported analysis of Cambridge samples gives no corpus, method, or complexity measure, so do not use it to teach a “simple language earns Band 9” rule. ([IELTS Writing preparation resources](https://ielts.org/take-a-test/preparation-resources/writing-test-resources); [Writing band descriptors](https://ielts.org/cdn/ielts-guides/ielts-writing-band-descriptors.pdf))
- The six-part essay taxonomy and the four-paragraph opinion scaffold are teaching aids, not official IELTS categories or required structures. A clear central topic within a paragraph is useful, but one claim per paragraph is not a mechanical rule.
- The three-part opinion introduction is a useful option for a prompt that asks for a position. For discussion or direct questions, make sure the introduction and body answer all requested parts rather than inserting an irrelevant opinion.
- Some source videos describe a single Writing criterion as 25% of the “total mark.” More precisely, IELTS assesses each task using four equally weighted criteria, and Task 2 carries twice the weight of Task 1. A grammar error does not automatically lower the Coherence and Cohesion criterion; assess each criterion on its own evidence. ([official Writing criteria](https://ielts.org/take-a-test/preparation-resources/writing-test-resources))
- Claims that most students lose a fixed band for not checking, that a teacher can write a Band 9 essay in 15 minutes, and that the process guarantees a desired result are not established in the lesson. Teach the routines, then use learner work to judge what improves.
- The companion describes its conclusion routine as three “essential” elements (a cohesive device, position, and summary) and promotes one of two linking phrases as something to memorize. Teach the useful response-and-recap function; a specific opener is optional, and the rubric does not require a fixed conclusion formula. Its story that a student’s lack of proofreading explained a band difference, its report of five-minute checks changing scores, and the claim that expert or former-examiner feedback is necessary are not independently established. ([1:48–3:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Rk8fjwbRGvQ&t=108s); [7:02–11:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Rk8fjwbRGvQ&t=422s))
- The 36-minute lesson’s three-pillar analogy is a useful way to teach paragraph development, not an official requirement that every paragraph use three fixed parts in that order. Its Tesla data-collection description, claims about how Tesla trains autonomous driving, and estimate that robots can save three weeks a year are not sourced in the video; do not repeat them as facts. Its “Band 8” and “Band 6.5” student labels and score-change stories are not independently verified. ([1:11–2:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rXVR-nE2jvw&t=71s); [27:42–30:33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rXVR-nE2jvw&t=1662s); [32:39–33:45](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rXVR-nE2jvw&t=1959s); [35:02–35:34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rXVR-nE2jvw&t=2102s))
- The video’s Cambridge-analysis anecdote, examiner headache story, VIP student outcome, limited-time discount, and claims about course success are not independently documented. Its free PDF and paid feedback offer are promotion, not syllabus evidence. ([8:05–8:18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NECR879vg-Y&t=485s), [10:13–11:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NECR879vg-Y&t=613s), [26:51–28:15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NECR879vg-Y&t=1611s))
- The 2026 companion’s 6.5-to-8 score story, “thousands of students” outcome, claim that the strategy is the only one learners need, and statements about how most students perform are not independently verified. Keep the prompt analysis, focused development, and error-led review; do not adopt its guarantees or exact planning and proofreading minutes as universal rules. Its sleep essay’s reported “recent study,” basketball-team example, and numerical work-hours comparison lack sources in the video and should be replaced with verified or clearly hypothetical examples before reuse. ([0:00–1:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aIqBxtrUodQ&t=0s), [12:37–17:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aIqBxtrUodQ&t=757s), [22:57–26:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aIqBxtrUodQ&t=1377s))
- The essay-walkthrough video’s “every question” and Band 7–9 outcome promises, claims about the instructor’s comparative success, and required-looking templates are not evidence that one outline guarantees a score. Teach prompt-specific coverage, paragraph development, and deliberate practice; include the structure as a scaffold only. ([0:00–1:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q_5jmvbwf-g&t=0s), [4:00–7:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q_5jmvbwf-g&t=240s))
- The 45-minute lesson's student is a worked example, not a verified band outcome. Its statements that a particular idea is what “90 of 100” people would say, that there is a simple route to a Band 8/9, and that structure plus Task Response make up half the score are not substantiated in the video. IELTS assesses Task Response, Coherence and Cohesion, Lexical Resource, and Grammatical Range and Accuracy equally within each Writing task; Task 2 has greater weight than Task 1. Replace the lesson’s unsupported reading-trend and platform examples with verified evidence or label them as hypothetical. ([5:00–8:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x-_vHUzm3b4&t=300s); [38:00–45:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x-_vHUzm3b4&t=2280s); [official Writing criteria](https://ielts.org/take-a-test/preparation-resources/writing-test-resources))
